subject: Critical Thinking
subcategory: Evidence & Truth: How We Know What's Real
title: The Problem of Induction: Can the Past Predict the Future?
description: Learn The Problem of Induction: Can the Past Predict the Future? in one minute.

hook.text: The sun has risen every day for 4.5 billion years. Does that prove it will rise tomorrow? David Hume said no.

buildup.text: Induction: drawing general conclusions from specific observations.

discovery.text: Hume's problem: induction assumes the future will resemble the past. But that assumption itself relies on induction.

twist.text: Then black swans were discovered in Australia.

climax.text: Science depends on induction but can't justify it logically.

punchline.text: The past doesn't guarantee the future. We just bet on it.

quiz.question: What is Hume's problem of induction?
options: We can't logically justify that the future will resemble the past

details.summary: The problem of induction, raised by David Hume, asks why we assume the future will resemble the past. Every inductive conclusion — the sun will rise tomorrow — is logically unjustifiable yet practically indispensable.
details.whyItMatters: The problem of induction reveals that even our most confident scientific predictions rest on an assumption that cannot itself be proven, which is a profound limitation of empirical knowledge.
takeaways: Induction assumes the future will resemble the past
This assumption cannot be logically justified without circularity
Science works despite the problem because induction is practically reliable

faq.question: Why can't we logically prove that the sun will rise tomorrow?
faq.answer: Proving it requires assuming nature is uniform, and that assumption is itself based on past observations. The argument becomes circular: the future will resemble the past because it always has. Hume showed this logical gap is inescapable.

faq.question: If induction cannot be logically justified, why does science still work?
faq.answer: Practically, induction works extraordinarily well. Bridges hold, medicines heal, and predictions succeed. The philosophical gap does not undermine practical reliability. Science operates on induction's track record, not logical certainty.
